explanation: Medications are used alongside therapy to control tough, disruptive symptoms—they aren't a standalone cure, but they offer great relief. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T1#GNS314_U2_T1_h6)

question: Early-onset conduct disorder in childhood is a major risk factor for which adult mental health condition?

options.A: Parkinson's disease
options.B: Alzheimer's dementia
options.C: Antisocial personality disorder
options.D: Obsessive-compulsive disorder

explanation: Severe conduct problems that begin early in life can unfortunately persist into adulthood as antisocial personality patterns if not addressed. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T1#GNS314_U2_T1_h7)

question: Which of these factors generally improves the long-term outlook for a child with a behaviour disorder?

options.A: Timely and consistent therapeutic intervention
options.B: Waiting until adulthood for natural maturity
options.C: Avoiding all contact with mental health professionals
options.D: Changing schools every single year

explanation: Early, structured support from healthcare providers and family gives the child much better coping skills for a bright future! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T1#GNS314_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the main goal of adaptive processes in our body and mind?

options.A: To eliminate all forms of emotional memory
options.B: To increase physical heart rate permanently
options.C: To prevent any future exposure to conflict
options.D: To restore internal balance during stress

explanation: Think of adaptive processes like your body's natural shock absorbers. They kick in to help you handle stress and bring your inner calm back! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h1)

question: As a psychiatric nurse, how should you view a patient's mental health symptoms when you first meet them?

options.A: As deliberate choices made to upset family members
options.B: As proof that the patient lacks all willpower
options.C: As an attempt by the psyche to protect itself
options.D: As permanent brain damage that cannot heal

explanation: Every symptom has a backstory. When we view symptoms as the mind's clumsy way of shielding itself from pain, it becomes much easier to care for our patients without judgment. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h1)

question: In mental health, what does 'primary gain' mean?

options.A: Internal relief from emotional anxiety
options.B: Financial rewards from health insurance
options.C: Extra attention given by family members
options.D: Physical strength gained from exercise

explanation: Primary gain happens right inside the mind. It is that secret, automatic relief you get when a symptom keeps scary or painful feelings tucked safely away from your conscious thoughts. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient loves the extra sympathy and gets excused from chores because of physical complaints that doctors can't find a medical cause for. What is this called?

options.A: Primary gain
options.B: Secondary gain
options.C: Cognitive dissonance
options.D: Neuroplasticity

explanation: Spot on! Secondary gain refers to the external perks—like extra care, sympathy, or getting out of house chores—that come along with playing the sick role. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which defense mechanism involves unconsciously pushing painful memories away so you don't have to think about them?

options.A: Repression
options.B: Sublimation
options.C: Regression
options.D: Projection

explanation: Repression is like sweeping painful memories under the mental rug without even realizing you're doing it. Out of sight, out of mind! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h3)

question: An angry nursing student wants to yell at a strict clinical instructor, but instead channels that energy into scrubbing the skill lab for hours. What defense mechanism is this?

options.A: Sublimation
options.B: Projection
options.C: Regression
options.D: Denial

explanation: That is sublimation! It is taking raw, unacceptable aggression and turning it into something super productive and socially acceptable. Cleaning counts as a win! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which system in the body pumps out stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline when you face a sudden scare?

options.A: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
options.B: The lymphatic fluid drainage system
options.C: The gastrointestinal digestive tract
options.D: The superficial integumentary system

explanation: It is a big mouthful to say, but the HPA axis is your body's master alarm system for stress. It floods your system with cortisol to get you ready for action! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why can unending, chronic stress eventually lead to long-term anxiety or panic?

options.A: Because the muscles permanently lose their ability to relax
options.B: Because repeated stress sensitizes the brain's fear circuits
options.C: Because the liver stops producing essential blood proteins
options.D: Because chronic worry completely destroys all brain neurons

explanation: When your brain's alarm system stays switched on for too long without a break, those fear pathways get stuck on high alert. That's neuroplasticity working against us! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is a major sign that a coping behavior is maladaptive rather than helpful?

options.A: It always improves personal relationships
options.B: It appears only once in a person's life
options.C: It is rigid and impairs daily functioning
options.D: It easily resolves without any outside help

explanation: Maladaptive habits are stuck on repeat. Instead of helping you solve a problem, they cause rigid roadblocks that make daily life and relationships harder. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h5)

question: A patient handles ward stress by going for brisk walks and talking things through with a close friend. How would a nurse label this response?

options.A: Psychotic
options.B: Adaptive
options.C: Regressive
options.D: Maladaptive

explanation: Spot on! Exercising and leaning on a support system are classic healthy, adaptive ways to handle pressure. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h5)

question: As a psychiatric nurse evaluating a patient's unusual symptom, what is the most important question to ask yourself?

options.A: How quickly can medication completely erase this behavior?
options.B: What is the exact medical billing code for this diagnosis?
options.C: Which family member caused the patient to act this way?
options.D: What purpose does this symptom serve for the patient?

explanation: Always look for the 'why.' Understanding what job the symptom is doing for the patient helps you uncover its protective or adaptive role. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which nursing diagnosis fits best when a patient struggles to use good defense mechanisms and falls back on unhealthy coping patterns?

options.A: Ineffective thermoregulation
options.B: Impaired physical mobility
options.C: Ineffective coping
options.D: Deficient fluid volume

explanation: When life stressors outweigh a person's current tools for handling them, 'Ineffective coping' is the exact NANDA diagnosis we reach for. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main goal of nursing care when we want to help a patient improve their adaptation skills?

options.A: To ensure the patient relies permanently on hospital staff
options.B: To eliminate all stress from the patient's external environment
options.C: To replace maladaptive habits with healthy coping skills
options.D: To force the patient to forget all past traumatic events

explanation: We can't wrap our patients in cotton wool or remove all stress. Our goal is to coach them toward flexible, healthy ways to weather life's storms! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which nursing action best helps a patient who is trying to overcome avoidance behaviors triggered by anxiety?

options.A: Supporting gradual exposure to feared situations
options.B: Encouraging deeper regression into dependent behaviors
options.C: Isolating the patient until anxiety disappears completely
options.D: Telling the patient to ignore all feelings of fear

explanation: Taking small, supported steps toward what scares them helps patients build confidence and rewrite their brain's alarm system safely. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T2#GNS314_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why do we classify mental health symptoms into categories?

options.A: To provide a permanent cure for mental illness
options.B: To replace the need for patient interviews
options.C: To replace laboratory testing in all hospitals
options.D: To organize complex symptoms into structured categories

explanation: Grouping similar symptoms together helps you make sense of a client's presentation so you can manage their care easily. You've got this! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the big benefit of the healthcare team using the same diagnostic terms?

options.A: It reduces the total cost of hospital administration
options.B: It allows clear communication and predictable care planning
options.C: It ensures patients never experience adverse drug reactions
options.D: It removes all personal bias from psychiatric nursing

explanation: When everyone on the ward speaks the same clinical language, patient handovers become smooth and clear. Great job thinking like a nurse! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h1)

question: What was a major headache with early psychiatric classification systems?

options.A: Governments refused to fund any mental health research
options.B: They focused exclusively on genetic markers
options.C: Too many laboratory tests were required for admission
options.D: Inconsistencies between hospitals caused clinical confusion

explanation: Back in the day, different hospitals used totally different terms. This made sharing notes or comparing treatments a real struggle! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h2)

question: Why do mental health diagnostic manuals keep getting updated?

options.A: To make nursing documentation twice as long to complete
options.B: To reflect new research and changing scientific understanding
options.C: To increase the total number of medications manufacturers sell
options.D: To erase all past history of psychiatric care

explanation: Science never stops growing! As we discover more about the human mind, manuals are updated so your nursing care stays top-notch. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which body publishes the famous Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)?

options.A: The American Psychiatric Association
options.B: The Global Nursing Council
options.C: The International Medical Association
options.D: The World Health Organization

explanation: The American Psychiatric Association develops and updates the DSM. Handy fact to keep tucked in your brain for exams! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h3)

question: A nurse checks a client's chart to see if their symptoms have lasted long enough to meet clinical guidelines. Which manual is she likely using?

options.A: The DSM-5-TR
options.B: The International Nursing Index
options.C: The Hospital Safety Manual
options.D: The British Pharmacopoeia

explanation: The DSM-5-TR gives exact timelines and severity checklists that clinicians use to match a client's symptoms. You're mastering psychiatric tools! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which global organization maintains the International Classification of Diseases (ICD)?

options.A: The American Nurses Association
options.B: The National Institute of Mental Health
options.C: The World Medical Board
options.D: The World Health Organization

explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes the ICD to track health trends and standardize medical diagnoses worldwide. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h4)

question: How does the ICD stand apart from the DSM?

options.A: The ICD ignores symptom duration when diagnosing mental health
options.B: The ICD covers all general medical conditions, not just mental disorders
options.C: The ICD is published by a local psychiatric association
options.D: The ICD is only used for nursing documentation in emergency rooms

explanation: While the DSM focuses purely on mental health, the ICD is a massive catalog covering every known human illness and injury. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which group of mental health conditions features overwhelming fear and ongoing distress?

options.A: Depressive and Bipolar Disorders
options.B: Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders
options.C: Anxiety and Trauma-Related Disorders
options.D: Personality Disorders

explanation: These disorders are tied to persistent fear, constant high alert, and stress linked to difficult life events. Keep building that clinical vocabulary! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the hallmark feature of personality disorders?

options.A: Severe memory loss caused by acute physical brain trauma
options.B: Rigid, enduring patterns of behavior differing from cultural norms
options.C: Sudden temporary episodes of visual and auditory hallucinations
options.D: Rapid daily shifts between severe mania and deep depression

explanation: Personality disorders involve long-term, inflexible ways of thinking and acting that make daily relationships and coping quite tough. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h5)

question: What does a categorical diagnostic approach assume about a client?

options.A: Every patient shares the exact same underlying brain chemistry
options.B: A person either has a specific disorder or does not
options.C: All psychological symptoms exist on an infinite sliding scale
options.D: Diagnosis should change daily based on mood

explanation: The categorical model views mental health conditions like a box: you either meet the criteria and have the diagnosis, or you don't. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which statement best captures the dimensional approach to mental health?

options.A: It measures symptom severity along a continuous spectrum
options.B: It ignores mild symptoms in favor of severe crises
options.C: It assigns every patient a rigid, permanent label
options.D: It relies solely on blood tests and imaging results

explanation: Instead of a simple yes-or-no box, the dimensional approach looks at how mild, moderate, or severe a client's symptoms are. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h6)

question: How does knowing a client's psychiatric diagnosis directly help you as a nurse?

options.A: It prevents the need to perform routine mental status checks
options.B: It allows the nurse to prescribe psychotropic medications independently
options.C: It guarantees the patient will be discharged within forty-eight hours
options.D: It provides a roadmap for anticipating safety risks and planning care

explanation: A diagnosis gives you a head start on what safety precautions and nursing interventions your client will need. Brilliant nursing insight! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h7)

question: A nurse is planning care for a newly admitted client with major depressive disorder. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Assume the client requires immediate physical restraints for agitation
options.B: Discontinue all monitoring since the diagnosis explains the behavior
options.C: Focus exclusively on teaching the client about complex surgical procedures
options.D: Assess the client for active suicidal ideation and ensure a safe environment

explanation: Safety first! Major depressive disorder means you must always screen for self-harm and keep the environment secure. You're thinking like a true professional. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is 'diagnostic overshadowing' in clinical practice?

options.A: Physical symptoms being incorrectly dismissed as psychological issues
options.B: Family members refusing to accept any medical diagnosis
options.C: A patient receiving two different psychiatric labels at the exact same time
options.D: A clinician forgetting to document the patient's primary complaint

explanation: Overshadowing happens when real physical sickness gets ignored simply because the patient has a mental health history. Always look at the whole person! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a common negative effect of psychiatric stigma?

options.A: Reluctance among clients to seek professional help
options.B: Social isolation within the community
options.C: Increased social support and faster recovery times
options.D: Internalized shame and lowered client self-esteem

explanation: Stigma hurts—it causes shame, isolation, and delays in getting care. It certainly doesn't speed up recovery! Spotting this makes you a compassionate nurse. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T3#GNS314_U2_T3_h8)

question: What are the three main categories in the biopsychosocial model?

options.A: Genetics, environment, and medication
options.B: Biological, psychological, and social factors
options.C: Emotional, behavioral, and cultural traits
options.D: Physical, spiritual, and financial factors

explanation: The biopsychosocial model organizes the causes of mental illness into three core dimensions: biological, psychological, and social. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is the biopsychosocial model especially useful in psychiatric nursing?

options.A: It helps nurses look at the whole person rather than just one symptom
options.B: It ensures that every patient receives the exact same treatment plan
options.C: It replaces the need for any laboratory testing or physical exams
options.D: It proves that all mental illnesses are caused by bad parenting

explanation: Because mental disorders have multiple roots, this model encourages nurses to assess physical, emotional, and social aspects of a patient's life for holistic care. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h1)

question: What does a genetic predisposition to a mental disorder mean?

options.A: The person will definitely develop the illness as they age
options.B: The illness cannot be treated with modern psychiatric medications
options.C: The condition was caused entirely by a poor diet in childhood
options.D: The person has a higher chance of developing the condition

explanation: Genetic predisposition means a person carries inherited vulnerabilities that make them more likely to develop a disorder if other triggers are present. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h2)

question: A patient is admitted with sudden, severe confusion and mood swings. What must the nurse consider first based on biological etiology?

options.A: Whether an underlying physical illness or hormone imbalance is causing the symptoms
options.B: How long the patient has been using herbal sleeping mixtures
options.C: Which family member caused the patient to feel stressed recently
options.D: If the patient experienced a difficult childhood in the village

explanation: Medical issues like thyroid problems or infections can cause psychiatric symptoms, so biological causes must be investigated during assessment. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily linked to feelings of reward, motivation, and the hallucinations seen in schizophrenia?

options.A: Dopamine
options.B: Melatonin
options.C: Serotonin
options.D: GABA

explanation: Dopamine pathways regulate reward and motivation, and overactive dopamine signaling is a major factor in psychotic symptoms like hallucinations. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary function of GABA in the central nervous system?

options.A: To trigger happy memories in the frontal lobe
options.B: To stimulate muscle movement in the arms and legs
options.C: To calm nervous system activity and reduce anxiety
options.D: To increase blood pressure during a physical threat

explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, meaning it slows down brain activity to keep anxiety levels manageable. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is a maladaptive coping mechanism?

options.A: A medical test used to check neurotransmitter levels
options.B: A healthy way of solving problems during a crisis
options.C: A strategy that makes stress harder to handle over time
options.D: A genetic trait passed down from parents to children

explanation: Maladaptive coping refers to unhealthy habits like avoidance or denial that provide temporary relief but worsen mental health in the long run. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h4)

question: How do early childhood attachment disruptions affect a person later in life?

options.A: They automatically cause physical brain damage within the first year
options.B: They can impair emotional regulation and increase vulnerability to stress
options.C: They guarantee that the person will develop schizophrenia as an adult
options.D: They prevent the individual from ever learning how to read or write

explanation: Unstable early relationships with caregivers can hinder a person's ability to trust others and manage intense emotions effectively as an adult. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is a common consequence of mental health stigma in many communities?

options.A: Government agencies automatically provide free housing for patients
options.B: Patients recover much faster without taking any medications
options.C: People hide their symptoms and delay seeking professional help
options.D: Traditional healers refuse to communicate with psychiatric nurses

explanation: Stigma creates shame and fear of discrimination, causing individuals and families to hide psychiatric symptoms instead of getting medical care. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h5)

question: A family brings their relative to a psychiatric clinic after months of visiting prayer houses for sudden aggressive behavior. What should the nurse understand about this situation?

options.A: The family clearly does not care about the patient's well-being at all
options.B: Traditional and religious methods always cure mental disorders completely
options.C: Cultural and spiritual beliefs heavily influence care-seeking pathways in Nigeria
options.D: The psychiatric nurse should scold the family for wasting precious time

explanation: Understanding that families often consult spiritual or traditional sources first helps nurses provide non-judgmental education and build trust. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h5)

question: In the diathesis-stress model, what does 'diathesis' refer to?

options.A: An underlying vulnerability or predisposition
options.B: The chemical name for antipsychotic drugs
options.C: A sudden environmental crisis or life event
options.D: A physical test used to measure brainwaves

explanation: Diathesis represents the biological or psychological vulnerability a person carries before a major stressor triggers an illness. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why might two people experience the exact same traumatic event, but only one develops PTSD?

options.A: They have different underlying vulnerabilities and coping resources
options.B: The person who stayed healthy must have taken secret vitamins
options.C: Psychological trauma only affects individuals with high blood pressure
options.D: Trauma never causes long-term mental health problems in adults

explanation: Individual differences in genetics, past experiences, and coping skills mean stress affects people differently based on the diathesis-stress model. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h6)

question: What does the term 'dual diagnosis' mean in psychiatric care?

options.A: A patient is evaluated by two different doctors on the same day
options.B: A patient has two different physical infections at the same time
options.C: A patient requires two different types of surgical operations
options.D: A patient has both a mental illness and a substance use disorder

explanation: Dual diagnosis describes individuals who experience a co-occurring psychiatric condition and substance use problem simultaneously. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why do some patients with anxiety or depression start using alcohol or illicit drugs?

options.A: To permanently cure their neurotransmitter imbalances
options.B: To strengthen their immune system against infectious diseases
options.C: Because healthcare providers forced them to take the substances
options.D: To self-medicate and temporarily escape their emotional distress

explanation: Many individuals turn to substances as a way to numb painful emotional symptoms, even though it eventually makes their mental health worse. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which action best reflects a comprehensive psychiatric nursing assessment?

options.A: Reviewing the patient's financial records to determine their income
options.B: Exploring the patient's biological, psychological, and social history
options.C: Asking only about the exact moment the patient started feeling sad
options.D: Focusing solely on laboratory blood test results and vital signs

explanation: A thorough nursing assessment investigates all areas of the biopsychosocial model to understand the full picture of the patient's condition. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h8)

question: A nurse is planning care for a newly admitted patient with severe depression and a history of job loss. What should the nursing care plan include?

options.A: Strict bed rest with zero communication until the patient asks for help
options.B: Telling the patient to forget about their job loss and think positively
options.C: Both biological treatments like medication and social support for coping with stress
options.D: Discharging the patient immediately before addressing any emotional issues

explanation: Because mental disorders have multiple causes, effective nursing care combines medical, psychological, and social interventions. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the main difference between normal, everyday worry and a true anxiety disorder?

options.A: Anxiety disorders have no physical symptoms, unlike normal stress.
options.B: Normal anxiety only occurs in children, while anxiety disorders only affect adults.
options.C: Normal anxiety requires prescription medication to resolve.
options.D: Normal anxiety fades after the threat passes, while an anxiety disorder is chronic and disrupts daily life.

explanation: You've got this! Normal worry comes and goes with life's stresses. An anxiety disorder sticks around, making everyday tasks really tough. Spotting this difference helps us know when a patient needs extra support. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h1)

question: A patient says they feel constantly terrified for no clear reason and cannot go to work. How should you as a nurse view this?

options.A: As a normal reaction to everyday life pressures that will resolve on its own
options.B: As a physical sign of a primary cardiac event rather than psychological distress
options.C: As an attention-seeking behavior requiring behavioral redirection
options.D: As an abnormal, pathological anxiety response that requires clinical evaluation

explanation: Great clinical thinking! When fear is constant, unprovoked, and stops someone from living their life, it goes way beyond normal worry and needs professional care. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which anxiety condition involves sudden, unexpected waves of intense terror and pounding heart palpitations?

options.A: Panic disorder
options.B: Specific phobia
options.C: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.D: Social anxiety disorder

explanation: Spot on! Panic disorder is famous for these sudden, scary attacks out of nowhere, leaving the person worried about when the next one might strike. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h2)

question: A patient refuses to leave their house because they are terrified of having a panic attack in public and not being able to escape. What is this called?

options.A: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.B: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
options.C: Agoraphobia
options.D: Social anxiety disorder

explanation: You nailed it. Agoraphobia is the fear of being trapped in public spaces where escape feels hard, which often leads people to stay safely inside their homes. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which brain chemical helps calm nerve activity and is often out of balance in people with anxiety?

options.A: Histamine
options.B: Acetylcholine
options.C: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Think of GABA as the brain's natural 'chill pill'! It's our main calming chemical, keeping our nervous system from going into overdrive. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h3)

question: How can severe stress or trauma in childhood affect a person later in life?

options.A: It has no lasting impact once the individual reaches maturity.
options.B: It only influences physical health rather than psychological well-being.
options.C: It can alter brain development and prime the nervous system to overreact to future stress.
options.D: It guarantees the person will develop panic disorder by early adulthood.

explanation: Early life stress can set our inner alarm systems to be extra sensitive, making it easier to feel overwhelmed by anxiety down the road. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h3)

question: When severe anxiety kicks off the 'fight-or-flight' response, which physical sign do you expect to see?

options.A: Constricted pupils
options.B: Slowed digestion with increased salivation
options.C: Decreased respiratory rate
options.D: Increased heart rate (tachycardia)

explanation: You got it! Adrenaline pumps through the body, making the heart beat fast and hard to get us ready to run or fight. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why do many patients having severe anxiety rush to the emergency clinic complaining of chest pain and dizziness?

options.A: Anxiety triggers physical symptoms that mimic serious medical conditions like heart trouble.
options.B: Patients prefer to hide their mental health struggles from healthcare providers.
options.C: Anxiety only affects internal organs and has no psychological components.
options.D: Medical clinics offer free counseling for psychiatric disorders.

explanation: Anxiety doesn't just feel mental—it feels very physical! Racing hearts and chest tightness feel so much like a heart attack that patients naturally seek emergency help first. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why must a nurse check thyroid levels and ask about substance use when assessing a patient for anxiety?

options.A: Substance use screens are legally required for every psychiatric admission.
options.B: Thyroid hormones directly destroy GABA receptors in the brain.
options.C: Thyroid medications are the primary cure for generalized anxiety disorder.
options.D: Medical conditions and substances can cause physical symptoms that mimic anxiety disorders.

explanation: Brilliant nursing assessment! Things like a hyperactive thyroid or too much caffeine can cause tremors and a racing heart, looking just like anxiety when it's actually something else. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h5)

question: During a mental check, which sign is most typical for a patient with moderate to severe anxiety?

options.A: Flat affect and delayed motor movements
options.B: Delusions of grandeur and unresponsiveness
options.C: Profound lethargy and deep sleepiness
options.D: Rapid speech and poor ability to concentrate

explanation: When anxiety is high, the brain is racing! Patients often talk fast, jump between thoughts, and find it really hard to focus on questions. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the main downside of using benzodiazepines for a long-term fix for anxiety?

options.A: Severe worsening of depressive symptoms within minutes
options.B: Immediate and permanent liver failure after one dose
options.C: Total lack of effectiveness for acute panic attacks
options.D: Risk of tolerance, dependence, and physical withdrawal

explanation: Benzodiazepines work fast, but they are habit-forming. Over time, the body gets used to them, leading to dependence and tough withdrawal if stopped suddenly. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why do doctors usually prescribe SSRIs instead of benzodiazepines for daily, long-term anxiety management?

options.A: SSRIs stop panic attacks within two minutes of taking the pill.
options.B: SSRIs treat underlying chronic anxiety safely over time without addiction risks.
options.C: SSRIs have zero side effects compared to other psychiatric drugs.
options.D: Benzodiazepines cause permanent brain damage in every patient.

explanation: You got it! SSRIs are much safer for everyday, long-term use because they manage anxiety steadily without the trap of physical addiction. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h6)

question: A patient is having a severe panic attack, breathing fast, and crying out in fear. What is your best first nursing action?

options.A: Hand the patient a stack of educational pamphlets about panic disorder.
options.B: Stay with the patient and speak in calm, short sentences while guiding their breathing.
options.C: Speak loudly and rapidly to snap the patient out of their panic state.
options.D: Leave the room immediately to give the patient privacy to calm down.

explanation: Wonderful nursing care! Your calm presence and steady, simple guidance help anchor a patient when their world feels like it's crashing down. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why is it so important to use short, simple sentences when talking to an extremely anxious patient?

options.A: Cognitive processing and concentration are impaired during high anxiety.
options.B: Anxious patients cannot read written words on a chart.
options.C: Short sentences replace the need for prescription medications.
options.D: Complex sentences trigger violent outbursts in psychiatric units.

explanation: Think about it like a computer with too many tabs open! When anxiety is through the roof, the brain can't process long, complicated instructions. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is a common complication when anxiety disorders are left untreated for many years?

options.A: Permanent loss of the ability to speak
options.B: Development of co-occurring depression and substance abuse
options.C: Complete immunity to all forms of psychological stress
options.D: Spontaneous cure of all medical health problems

explanation: Carrying heavy, unmanaged anxiety wears down a person's emotional strength over time, often opening the door to depression or unhealthy coping habits. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h8)

question: Which lifestyle habit should you recommend to a patient trying to manage chronic anxiety?

options.A: Drinking several energy drinks daily to boost energy
options.B: Limiting caffeine intake and establishing regular sleep routines
options.C: Working night shifts to avoid social interaction
options.D: Eliminating all physical exercise from the daily schedule

explanation: Spot on! Caffeine is a stimulant that can mimic or worsen panic, while good sleep helps keep the nervous system balanced and steady. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T5#GNS314_U2_T5_h8)

question: What is the main difference between a normal fear and a phobia?

options.A: A phobia only happens during sleep
options.B: A normal fear never causes physical symptoms
options.C: A normal fear lasts for many years
options.D: A phobia is out of proportion to any actual danger

explanation: Phobias involve an extreme and irrational reaction that does not match the real level of threat present. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h1)

question: A student gets a sudden feeling of dread thinking about an upcoming exam next week. What is the best nursing term for this feeling?

options.A: Agoraphobia
options.B: Anxiety
options.C: Panic attack
options.D: Phobia

explanation: Anxiety is that generalized feeling of worry about future events. Unlike a specific, sudden trigger, it's just your mind working overtime about what's ahead! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a specific phobia?

options.A: Fear of heights
options.B: Fear of social judgment
options.C: Fear of leaving the house
options.D: Fear of public speaking

explanation: Fear of heights (acrophobia) is a classic specific phobia tied to a distinct environmental trigger. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why is agoraphobia often closely tied to panic attacks?

options.A: Agoraphobia only occurs immediately after a heart attack
options.B: Panic attacks always cure agoraphobia over time
options.C: Patients with agoraphobia never feel anxious in crowds
options.D: Patients fear they cannot escape easily if panic strikes

explanation: Agoraphobia is all about dreading public spaces where escaping or getting help during a sudden panic wave would feel impossible. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h2)

question: What do we call learning to fear something simply by watching how other people react to it?

options.A: Reading a medical textbook about anxiety
options.B: Developing a fear directly from a physical injury
options.C: Learning to fear something by watching others react with fear
options.D: Inheriting a phobia gene from a grandparent

explanation: This is observational learning! If a child sees a parent scream at the sight of a lizard, the child might pick up that exact same fear just by watching. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h3)

question: A patient develops a severe fear of water after nearly drowning as a child. What caused this phobia?

options.A: Genetic inheritance
options.B: Observational learning
options.C: Traumatic direct experience
options.D: Information transmission

explanation: A direct, frightening personal encounter with a danger leaves a strong impression, making it a classic direct trauma experience. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which part of the brain is the main control center for processing fear and triggering our fight-or-flight alarm?

options.A: Medulla oblongata
options.B: Cerebellum
options.C: Amygdala
options.D: Pituitary gland

explanation: Think of the amygdala as your brain's emotional smoke detector. It spots danger and sounds the alarm right away! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h4)

question: How does negative reinforcement keep a phobia going over time?

options.A: Taking medication increases the fear response every morning
options.B: Avoiding the feared object gives quick relief, making future avoidance more likely
options.C: Confronting the fear makes the anxiety disappear forever
options.D: Punishment from family members stops the patient from getting better

explanation: When you run away from what scares you, you feel instant relief. That brief relief rewards the escape behavior, making you more likely to run away again next time. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h4)

question: Blood-injection-injury phobias are quite unique. What physical reaction makes them different from other phobias?

options.A: Sudden paralysis of the lower limbs
options.B: Continuous muscle spasms in the face
options.C: An extreme increase in body temperature
options.D: A drop in blood pressure that leads to fainting

explanation: Most phobias send your heart rate racing, but blood and needle phobias often cause a sudden drop in blood pressure and heart rate, leading to good old fainting! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h5)

question: A patient with a terrible dog phobia suddenly sees a dog outside the clinic window. What physical sign is the nurse most likely to spot?

options.A: Rapid heart rate and trembling
options.B: Slurred speech and confusion
options.C: Low fever and joint swelling
options.D: Extreme sleepiness and lethargy

explanation: Seeing the trigger fires up the sympathetic nervous system. Expect tachycardia (fast heart rate), shaking, and pure adrenaline in action! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h5)

question: A patient is having a full panic attack due to a phobia. What should be the nurse's very first priority?

options.A: Leave the patient alone so they can calm down in private
options.B: Force the patient to face the fear source immediately
options.C: Help the patient feel safe and lower immediate anxiety
options.D: Teach complex problem-solving skills during the peak of panic

explanation: When panic peaks, keep it simple. Stay calm, be present, and focus on helping them feel secure until the storm passes. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which of these is a very common nursing diagnosis for a patient struggling with a severe phobia?

options.A: Impaired Gas Exchange
options.B: Deficient Fluid Volume
options.C: Risk for Infection
options.D: Ineffective Coping

explanation: Because phobias rely heavily on avoidance rather than healthy problem-solving, 'Ineffective Coping' fits right in your care plan. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is systematic desensitization in simple terms?

options.A: Gradual exposure to a feared trigger combined with relaxation techniques
options.B: Taking high doses of sedatives to forget the fear exists
options.C: Sudden and prolonged exposure to the most severe phobia trigger
options.D: Surgical removal of the memory of the trauma

explanation: It's a step-by-step ladder! You pair deep relaxation with small, manageable steps toward the scary thing until it doesn't scare you anymore. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why might a nursing student take a beta-blocker like propranolol before giving a major class presentation?

options.A: To increase their energy levels and stage presence
options.B: To cure their underlying social phobia permanently
options.C: To prevent them from falling asleep during the performance
options.D: To control physical symptoms like a racing heart and tremors

explanation: Beta-blockers block adrenaline, keeping your hands steady and heart calm without making your mind foggy. A real lifesaver for stage fright! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h7)

question: A family member asks how to help a relative overcome a bad driving phobia. What is the best advice to give?

options.A: Do all the driving for them so they never feel anxious again
options.B: Insist they drive on busy highways immediately to get over it
options.C: Hide all car keys so they forget about driving completely
options.D: Encourage small steps of progress and avoid enabling total avoidance

explanation: Doing everything for them (enabling) makes the phobia stronger. Families should cheer on small, brave steps forward instead! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h8)

question: Which common everyday drink should patients with anxiety and phobias cut back on because it triggers jitters and a fast heart rate?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Caffeine
options.C: Complex carbohydrates
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Caffeine is a stimulant. Too much coffee or energy drink can easily mimic or worsen panic symptoms like a racing pulse and shaky hands. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h8)

question: What is an obsession in someone dealing with obsessive-compulsive neurosis?

options.A: A physical movement done to relieve muscle tension
options.B: An intrusive and unwanted thought that causes anxiety
options.C: A sudden memory loss regarding personal identity
options.D: A complete loss of contact with external reality

explanation: Spot on! Think of an obsession as an unwelcome thought or image that keeps popping into the mind against the person's will, bringing along a lot of stress. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h1)

question: How do compulsions usually help a patient dealing with this condition?

options.A: They are physical exercises prescribed to improve general body tone
options.B: They serve as temporary relief from the anxiety caused by obsessions
options.C: They are creative hobbies used to express hidden artistic talents
options.D: They help the patient hallucinate pleasant images to pass the time

explanation: You got it! Compulsions are the repeated actions patients feel forced to do just to calm down the heavy anxiety sparked by their obsessions. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which of these behaviors is a classic example of a checking compulsion?

options.A: Washing the hands with soap for over an hour after touching a doorknob
options.B: Arranging clothing items in strict color-coded order inside a closet
options.C: Repeatedly verifying that the house doors are locked before sleeping
options.D: Silently repeating a specific religious phrase to undo a bad thought

explanation: Well done! Checking means going back over and over again to make sure things like locks or appliances are secure, just to feel safe. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h2)

question: A patient spends hours washing their hands until the skin is raw, driven by a deep fear of germs. What does this behavior represent?

options.A: A somatic symptom disorder caused by nerve damage
options.B: A psychotic delusion regarding skin parasites
options.C: A compulsion driven by an obsession with contamination
options.D: Normal hygienic practice during an infection outbreak

explanation: Correct! The excessive washing is a physical compulsion born out of an overwhelming fear of getting contaminated. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which brain chemical is most closely linked to obsessive-compulsive neurosis?

options.A: Serotonin
options.B: Histamine
options.C: Epinephrine
options.D: Acetylcholine

explanation: Spot on! Serotonin imbalance is the main chemical theory behind OCD, which is why medications targeting serotonin work so well. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is the main job of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical brain circuit in OCD?

options.A: Controlling voluntary muscle movement in the upper extremities
options.B: Producing visual images during rapid eye movement sleep
options.C: Filtering sensory information and regulating behavioral habits
options.D: Regulating body temperature and fluid balance in the kidneys

explanation: You nailed it! When this pathway has trouble filtering routine signals, the brain gets stuck in repetitive loops of thoughts and actions. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is a key time-based rule for diagnosing obsessive-compulsive neurosis?

options.A: Behaviors must last continuously for at least five full years
options.B: The episodes must happen only once every month without fail
options.C: The rituals must occur strictly during morning hours upon waking
options.D: Symptoms must take up more than one hour daily or cause marked distress

explanation: Correct! For a formal diagnosis, these thoughts or rituals usually need to steal over an hour of the patient's day or cause serious distress. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why do healthcare providers check a patient's level of insight during diagnosis?

options.A: It helps determine if the patient recognizes their beliefs as irrational
options.B: It shows if the family history contains genetic markers for depression
options.C: It proves whether the patient is physically capable of walking unaided
options.D: It measures the exact chemical levels of serotonin in the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! Checking insight lets us know if the patient realizes their fears are over-the-top, which helps shape how we plan their care. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which class of medication is usually given first for obsessive-compulsive neurosis?

options.A: Tricyclic muscle relaxants
options.B: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors
options.C: Short-acting barbiturate sedatives
options.D: Atypical antipsychotic medications

explanation: You got it! SSRIs are the go-to drugs to help balance serotonin levels and dial down those intense symptoms. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the main idea behind Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) therapy?

options.A: Using hypnosis to erase painful childhood memories from the mind
options.B: Prescribing high-dose sedatives to keep the patient calm and asleep
options.C: Encouraging the patient to indulge fully in rituals until they get tired
options.D: Exposing the patient to feared triggers while blocking compulsive rituals

explanation: Well done! ERP retrains the brain by facing what triggers the anxiety head-on, while gently holding off on the safety ritual. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h5)

question: A patient spends an hour doing a hand-washing ritual before meals. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Allow time for the ritual initially, then work with the patient to gradually set limits
options.B: Immediately shut off the water supply and force the patient to sit at the table
options.C: Administer a stat dose of intravenous antipsychotic medication to stop the habit
options.D: Scold the patient firmly to teach them that the behavior is completely useless

explanation: Spot on! Never cut them off cold turkey right away. Give them time at first, then gently help them reduce it over time. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid abruptly stopping a patient's compulsive ritual?

options.A: It immediately destroys the therapeutic trust built with the doctor
options.B: It breaks hospital legal regulations regarding patient property rights
options.C: It causes permanent physical paralysis in the patient's limbs
options.D: It triggers severe panic and dangerous anxiety spikes in the patient

explanation: Correct! Compulsions are their current shield against panic; snatching that away suddenly throws them into massive distress. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T7#GNS314_U2_T7_h6)

question: Which condition often develops later if obsessive-compulsive neurosis is left untreated?

options.A: Antisocial personality disorder
options.B: Schizoaffective disorder
options.C: Major depressive disorder
options.D: Dissociative identity disorder

question: What is the main benefit of Omega-3 fatty acids for mental health?

question: Why are art and creative therapies so helpful for trauma survivors?

question: How does music therapy help an agitated patient with dementia?

question: What is the nurse's main role when a patient wants to use alternative therapies?

question: Which option best describes a holistic psychiatric care plan?

question: What is the primary purpose of a downward referral in mental health?

question: A client with schizophrenia is stable and ready for discharge from a tertiary psychiatric hospital. What should the nurse do next?
